entry.title: I'm finally fine-tuning my model, because its prompt hit 175,000 characters
entry.summary: Line 60 of my model's prompt says "Never output em-dashes, in any form." Line 976 says it again, in case it forgot. The agent it runs in says it a third time. It still slips them in, so that agent ends up ripping them out of every reply in code, a token at a time, as it streams. That's when I admitted the prompt had gotten out of hand. Every version of Onyx, the model behind my local AI agent Flash, has secretly been a prompt. Not fine-tuned weights. A Modelfile wrapped around an open-weights base, with the system prompt doing all the work. Every time Onyx did something dumb, I wrote a rule. Onyx 2.6's prompt is now 174,826 characters long. That's about 980 lines of rules the model has to keep in mind while it works, and every new chat pays for all of them before it writes its first word. …

The Big Picture: From Text to Natural‑Sounding Voice
If you’ve ever wondered how a string of characters magically becomes a human‑like utterance, you’re not alone. Modern neural text‑to‑speech (TTS) systems have come a long way from the robotic “speak” of the 90s. Under the hood they combine three big ideas: Acoustic modeling – a deep network predicts a spectrogram (a visual representation of sound frequencies) from raw text.
Vocoder synthesis – another network turns that spectrogram into an audio waveform.

entry.title: Dynamic Multi-Level Loading in GDevelop (Without Duplicating Scenes)
entry.summary:
If you’re building a multi-level game in GDevelop, you do not need a separate scene for every stage. There’s a pattern using global variables and external layouts that keeps your entire game running on a single reusable scene.
Here’s how it works at a high level. One global variable drives everything. Create a number variable called current_level in your project’s global variables. Initialize it to 1. This is your level pointer. External layouts hold level geometry. Instead of new scenes, you create external layouts named with a consistent pattern — Level1, Level2, Level3, etc. Each layout uses your main game scene as its base, so it has access to all existing objects. Dynamic loading at scene start. In your main scene’s event sheet, add a “Beginning of scene” event with the action “Create objects from external layout.” The layout name is an expression: "Level" + GlobalVariableString(current_level) Set X, Y, Z origin to 0. Add a Trigger Once condition so it doesn’t fire every frame. Level transitions. When the player collides with a door and presses the interact key, increment current_level by 1 and change to the same scene. The scene reloads, the beginning-of-scene event fires, and the next layout gets pulled in automatically. Don’t forget camera boundaries. If your levels are different sizes, you need per-level camera boundary logic. Check the value of current_level and set boundaries accordingly, or your camera will float off into empty space. This pattern scales well — I’ve used it on projects with 20+ levels and the project file stays manageable. No duplicated event sheets, no object sprawl across scenes. I made a video walkthrough that covers the full implementation if you prefer to see it built step by step: https://youtu.be/KBtNvKsRlwk
